title: Hemkunt Sahib
hook: a high Himalayan lake linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's former life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, and the Sohila's wedding song. Your line was ashes to the river. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand three hundred forty.

For part of every year, snow closes the path. When it opens, pilgrims climb on foot, or on ponies, up a steep trail in the Himalayas, past waterfalls and wildflowers, breathing hard in the thin air. At the top there's a lake, clear and very cold, ringed by peaks, and on its shore a gurdwara. Some pilgrims step into that icy water. The place is called Hemkunt Sahib, and Sikh tradition ties it to a life before the Tenth Guru's life.
screen: `SNOW CLOSES THE PATH.` → `A STEEP CLIMB, THIN AIR.` → `A COLD LAKE, A GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: First, the text. In the Bachittar Natak, a work in the Dasam Granth that Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh, the poet tells his own story. In paraphrase: in an earlier life, he did deep austerity on a mountain called Hemkunt, a place of peaks, absorbed in God, until God called him to be born into the world and spread the right way of living. He says, in paraphrase, that he did not want to come, his mind was so joined to God's feet, but God sent him. Second, the finding. The poem names Hemkunt, but doesn't give a map. Long after the Guru, Sikhs identified this lake in the Himalayas as the Hemkunt of the poem, and a gurdwara was built on its shore. Third, the honest part. Sikhs hold different views here. Some read the passage as the Guru's literal memory of a former life. Some read it as poetry about a calling. Some Sikhs also discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth are the Guru's own. This path describes these views; it doesn't decide. Fourth, what the pilgrims do with it. Whatever they think of the map, they climb. The trail is hard, and they climb it anyway. And at the top, the poem's picture becomes something you can stand in: a still place, high up, close to the sky, where someone, tradition says, was so happy with God that he didn't want to leave. And left anyway, because he was sent.
screen: `THE BACHITTAR NATAK'S STORY.` · `A LAKE IDENTIFIED, LONG AFTER.` · `LITERAL MEMORY, OR POETRY?` · `THE CLIMB.` · then, large: `THE HIGH LAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a mountain lake. Settle, and breathe. See the water: very still, very clear, the color of the sky. Peaks stand all around it, white at the top. The air is cold and thin, so your breath goes slow on its own. Sit at the edge. Nothing to do here. Then remember the poem: someone happy in a place like this, called to go down into the busy world. Let your breath carry a little of the stillness down with you. The bell holds the time.
Hemkunt Sahib. The high Himalayan lake and gurdwara that Sikhs identify with the Hemkunt of the Bachittar Natak, where the poem places the Tenth Guru's former life. Today's word.
Your line: the high lake. Today, before you walk into something busy, stop at the door for one still breath, and carry it in. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: When the snow clears, Sikh pilgrims climb the steep trail to Hemkunt Sahib, bathe in the cold lake, and join the Ardas and kirtan at the gurdwara on its shore.

original.note: the name of the mountain in the Bachittar Natak, and of the lake Sikhs identify with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hemkunt is where the Tenth Guru lived.
what it means: the Bachittar Natak places a former life of austerity at Hemkunt, before his birth.
what a scholar hears: the poem gives no map; the lake was identified long after, and Sikhs read the passage in more than one way.
recall: one who walks on Nanak's path

notes: Bachittar Natak, adhiai 6 ('ab mai apnee kathaa bakhaano, tap saadhat jih bidh muhi aano; hemkunt parbat hai jahaa, sapat sring sobhit hai tahaa...') paraphrased; 'sapat sring' (seven peaks) is rendered as 'a place of peaks' to avoid a number. Please confirm the chapter and paraphrase.
The passage on not wanting to come ('ham na bhajan ko chaahat ...' / 'chit na bhayo hamro aavan kah') is paraphrased; please confirm.

Authorship of the Dasam Granth is described neutrally ('Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh'; 'some Sikhs discuss which parts are the Guru's own'). Please confirm the framing is fair to all views.
The identification of the lake (in the twentieth century, by Sant Sohan Singh and Havildar Modan Singh, in many accounts) is given only as 'long after the Guru'. Please confirm.
'For much of the year, nobody can get there' is a general claim about seasonal closure; please confirm or soften.
The trail mention of 'ponies' and 'wildflowers' is general description; please confirm.
